disease_info: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is characterized by one or more major depressive episodes lasting at least two weeks, involving persistent low mood and/or markedly diminished interest or pleasure, accompanied by cognitive, somatic, and behavioral changes such as altered sleep, appetite, energy, concentration, and self-worth. Clinically, it requires significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning, and cannot be better explained by substances, medical conditions, normal bereavement, or bipolar-spectrum mood episodes. The course can be single-episode or recurrent, with episodes often triggered by psychosocial stressors but sometimes emerging without clear precipitants, especially in individuals with biological vulnerability. It is distinguished from adjustment disorders by severity and symptom constellation, and from bipolar disorder by the absence of manic or hypomanic episodes.

narrative.personality: Bernice is a meticulous, nurturing organizer with a rich imaginative life who pours herself into creative arts and community storytelling.
narrative.stressor: Bernice’s depressive episode began to take shape about a year after the death of her husband, when the flurry of immediate support from church and family had faded and she found herself alone in a quiet house most evenings. As the senior community organizer, she kept pushing herself to run quilting circles and storytelling events, but small mistakes in planning and the occasional missed detail started to weigh on her disproportionally, stirring up old memories of growing up poor and “being a burden.” Over several months she gradually withdrew from some of her beloved workshops and stopped initiating visits with the younger women she mentored, spending more time ruminating on whether she had done enough for her late husband and whether her life’s work truly mattered. She finally agreed to see a psychiatrist after a church friend noticed she had given away several cherished quilts, repeatedly described herself as “useless now that he’s gone,” and broke down in tears during a planning meeting, insisting every past misstep in her marriage and family was her fault.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t shake this feeling that I failed my husband and my family, like my whole life hasn’t amounted to much.”

narrative.personality: Dwayne is a methodical, practically minded retiree who takes pride in precision and enjoys mentoring others through woodworking and community projects.
narrative.stressor: About nine months ago, Dwayne underwent an unexpected cardiac procedure after a routine checkup revealed significant blockage, forcing him to cut back abruptly on the physically demanding aspects of his woodworking and volunteer work. Accustomed to being the reliable, hands-on problem-solver, he struggled with the new limitations, especially when his doctor advised against lifting heavy lumber and long shifts at the community kitchen. Over time, his days became less structured: he started staying up later, dozing in his chair, and lying awake for hours replaying medical conversations and worrying about being a burden on his wife, which eroded his usual enjoyment of projects and social games like bridge. His wife eventually persuaded him to seek psychiatric help when she noticed that his sleep had become chronically disrupted, he was napping unpredictably, and he admitted that his nights were now dominated by restless, anxious brooding about his health and future.
narrative.chief_complaint: “My sleep’s all over the place now—I’m up half the night and can’t seem to get any real rest.”

narrative.personality: Craig is a laid-back yet conscientious supervisor who values structure at work but prefers solitary, quietly rebellious hobbies in his personal time.
narrative.stressor: Craig’s difficulties began after his retail chain underwent a major restructuring about a year ago, bringing in a new regional manager who emphasized aggressive sales targets and constant performance metrics. The collaborative, mentorship-focused environment he had cultivated over decades was replaced by pressure to cut hours and enforce policies he felt were unfair to long-time staff, leading to ongoing conflicts between his values and what was being demanded of him. Over several months, he started staying later at the store to cover staffing gaps and handle complaints, then coming home too drained to set up his model trains, tend the garden, or spin records—activities that had always been his way of recharging. When his spouse pointed out that weekends were now spent mostly on the couch with the TV on and that he hadn’t touched his model railroad layout or signed up for food pantry shifts in months, Craig recognized that he no longer felt drawn to the pastimes that once defined him and agreed to see a psychiatrist.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I just don’t care about the things I used to love doing anymore—nothing really interests me now.”
